issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising restricted revisional jurisdiction after an appeal cannot set aside a lower court’s decision merely because it considers a finding of fact or law erroneous.
material_facts: The landlords obtained an eviction order on the ground that the house was bona fide required for reconstruction, and the District Court dismissed the tenant’s appeal.
The tenant’s revision challenged the findings that reconstruction was required and that the landlords acted bona fide.
The statutory proviso restricted the High Court’s revisional powers in a case where an appeal lay to the District Court.
issues.conclusion: The challenged merits findings did not permit the High Court to interfere in revision; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 17(1) of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, as restricted by its proviso where an appeal lies under Section 15, the High Court’s powers are equivalent to those under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and extend to jurisdictional errors, not mere errors of fact or law. The Court relied on Neta Ram v. Jiwan Lal; Wora Abbasbhai Alimahomed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Safibhai; Balakrishna Udayar v. Vasudeva Aiyar; A. Batchamain Sahib and Co. v. A.N. Channiah; and Hari Shanker v. Girdhari Lal.

predicates.revision_follows_an_appeal: A party pursued an appeal from a lower court’s decision and then sought revision of the appellate decision.
predicates.lower_court_decided_within_its_jurisdict: The lower court had authority to decide the matter before it and decided it.
predicates.challenge_is_only_to_a_factual_or_legal_: The challenge alleges that the court reached the wrong factual or legal conclusion, without identifying a jurisdictional defect.

issues.definition: When revision follows an appeal, the lower court decided within its authority, and the challenge concerns only the merits, the reviewing court cannot correct that error in revision.

issues.legal_issue: A court’s allegedly mistaken finding that a landlord bona fide requires possession does not itself constitute a jurisdictional error when the court has found the statutory requirement satisfied.
material_facts: The eviction application relied on the landlords’ bona fide need to carry out reconstruction that could not be done without the house being vacated.
The tenant argued that the landlords’ statement that the reconstructed accommodation might not suit the tenant showed that the reconstruction claim was not bona fide.
The courts below granted eviction after finding the landlords’ requirement established.
issues.conclusion: An allegedly wrong finding on bona fides did not involve an error pertaining to jurisdiction and could not support interference under the restricted revisional power.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(2)(ix) of the Mysore House Rent and Accommodation Control Act, 1951, permits eviction on this ground when the court is satisfied that the landlord bona fide requires the house for repairs or reconstruction that cannot be carried out without it being vacated. That satisfaction is the condition conferring authority to order eviction; once the court records satisfaction, a mistaken conclusion on bona fides is not, merely for that reason, a jurisdictional error. The restricted revisional principles under Section 17 and Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure apply.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under a statutory rent-control process.
predicates.eviction_ground_requires_bona_fide_satis: The asserted ground permits eviction only if the deciding court is satisfied that the landlord genuinely requires possession for the stated purpose.
predicates.court_found_requirement_satisfied: The deciding court found that the landlord’s required possession was established.
predicates.challenge_is_only_to_the_bona_fide_findi: The tenant alleges that the court was wrong about the genuineness of the landlord’s requirement, without showing a separate jurisdictional defect.

issues.definition: In a rent-eviction proceeding, when the court finds the required genuine need established, an allegation that this finding was wrong does not itself make the decision jurisdictionally defective.
